did_you_know.text: The word “ha-negeva” means “toward the south” and is related to the name of the Negev region. So the verse need not refer only to a specific place called the Negev.

In the Bible, the word “heavy” can also describe someone who is wealthy and owns a great deal, not only something with physical weight. Here, Abram’s wealth is described through livestock, silver, and gold.
The story reflects the life of nomadic herders: land and pasture are limited, and when the flocks grow, one group can no longer live comfortably in one place.
In the Bible, when a person faces east, north is on the left and south is on the right. Thus, “left” and “right” in this verse also indicate geographic directions.

“The Plain of the Jordan” was a broad area in the Jordan Valley, described as especially well-watered and fertile. Comparing it to the garden of the Lord and to Egypt emphasizes the abundance Lot saw.
“The terebinths of Mamre” is the name of a place near Hebron; the word for “terebinths” is connected with large trees, such as oaks or terebinths. Hebron is one of the ancient cities of the region.
